title: Ὀρνιθοθήρας καὶ πέρδιξ
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 285. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ὀρνιθοθήρας, ὀψιαίτερον αὐτῷ ξένου παραγενομένου, μὴ ἔχων ὅ τι αὐτῷ παραθείη, ὥρμησεν ἐπὶ τὸν τιθασσὸν πέρδικα καὶ τοῦτον θύειν ἔμελλε.
sentences.tr: Ornithothēras, opsiaiteron autōi xenou paragenomenou, mē echōn ho ti autōi paratheiē, hōrmēsen epi ton tithasson perdika kai touton thyein emelle.
sentences.l: A fowler, a guest having come to him rather late, having nothing that he might set before him, made for the tame partridge and was about to sacrifice it.
sentences.i: A fowler, when a guest arrived at his house rather late and he had nothing to set before him, made for his tame partridge and was on the point of killing it.
sentences.n: ὅ τι … παραθείη keeps a deliberative question inside a relative clause — 'what am I to set before him?' — and after a past-tense frame the deliberative subjunctive becomes optative: 'nothing that he might set before him', that is, nothing to serve. θύω is properly to sacrifice, and killing an animal for the table was in Greek practice a sacrifice; the idiomatic line says plainly what happens to the bird. The ξένος is the guest-friend, whose entertainment was a binding obligation — which is what puts the fowler in this difficulty at all.

sentences.t: Τοῦ δὲ αἰτιωμένου αὐτὸν ὡς ἀχάριστον, εἴγε πολλὰ ὠφελούμενος παρ’ αὐτοῦ τοὺς ὁμοφύλους ἐκκαλουμένου καὶ παραδιδόντος, αὐτὸς ἀναιρεῖν αὐτὸν μέλλει, ἔφη· « Ἀλλὰ διὰ τοῦτό σε μᾶλλον θύσω, εἰ μηδὲ τῶν ὁμοφύλων ἀπέχῃ. »
sentences.tr: Tou de aitiōmenou auton hōs achariston, eige polla ōpheloumenos par’ autou tous homophylous ekkaloumenou kai paradidontos, autos anairein auton mellei, ephē· « Alla dia touto se mallon thysō, ei mēde tōn homophylōn apechēi. »
sentences.l: And when it charged him with being ungrateful, in that, though greatly benefited by it, as it calls out its own kind and hands them over, he himself is about to make away with it, he said: « But for this reason I shall sacrifice you all the more, if you do not even hold off from your own kind. »
sentences.i: And the partridge charged him with ingratitude, seeing that he had profited greatly by it, since it called its own kind out and delivered them up, and yet was now about to make away with it; but he said: « That is all the more reason for me to kill you, if you will not even spare your own kind. »
sentences.n: The tame partridge is a decoy, kept to call wild birds within reach of the nets — the same arrangement as the tame doves of fable 282. ὠφελούμενος is nominative and belongs to the fowler; the genitives ἐκκαλουμένου and παραδιδόντος hang on παρ’ αὐτοῦ and belong to the partridge, so the sentence keeps both parties in view at once. εἴγε again gives the ground of the charge, as at fable 282. ἀπέχομαι with the genitive is 'hold off from'.

sentences.t: Ὁ λόγος δηλοῖ ὅτι οἱ τοὺς οἰκείους προδιδόντες οὐ μόνον ὑπὸ τῶν ἀδικουμένων μισοῦνται, ἀλλὰ καὶ ὑπὸ τούτων οἷς προδίδονται.
sentences.tr: Ho logos dēloi hoti hoi tous oikeious prodidontes ou monon hypo tōn adikoumenōn misountai, alla kai hypo toutōn hois prodidontai.
sentences.l: The story shows that those who betray their own people are hated not only by those who are wronged, but also by those to whom their own are betrayed.
sentences.n: ὑπό with the genitive names the agent of a passive, twice over here. In οἷς προδίδονται the dative is the party the betrayal is made to, and the unexpressed subject of the passive is the οἰκεῖοι who are handed over, not the betrayers themselves.
